newsitem.title: INDIA: INDIA RUPEE - Float means breaking of deficit chains.
newsitem.headline: INDIA RUPEE - Float means breaking of deficit chains.

text.p: India needs to cut through a macroeconomic knot comprised of multi-layered deficits and giant subsidy bills to achieve fiscal targets mapped out on the rupee's road to capital account convertibility.
A committee appointed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) earlier this month submitted its recommendations for a convertible rupee by the turn of the century.
The panel listed various preconditions needed before India fulfils its plans of a fully convertible rupee.

Those included an average inflation rate of three to five percent for the three year period until 2000, and a reduction in the fiscal deficit to gross domestic domestic (GDP) ratio to 3.5 percent by financial year 1999/2000 ending March 31.
The rupee was made convertible on the current account of the balance of payments in August 1994.

"These targets are like a mantra for the government which will keep on chanting it. These are not sustainable," said Jayati Ghosh, an economist who teaches at the New Delhi's Jawaharlal Nehru University.
India aims to cut the federal fiscal deficit to 4.5 percent of GDP in 1997/98 (April-March) from 5.0 percent last year.
Analysts said the key issue was the combined deficit of the federal and the states, estimated to be over 10 percent of GDP.
The World Bank in its Country Economic Memorandum in August 1996 said: "The consolidated deficit of the central government, state and public enterprises amounts to about 10 percent of GDP."
While the federal government has tried to put its house in order, the fiscal imbalance of the states and the state-owned enterprises has remain unaltered, the Bank said.

"It is difficult to reduce the deficit of the states," said S.P. Gupta, director of Indian Council for Research on International Economic Relations (ICRIER). "The fiscal deficit target is not sacrosanct."
A sudden compression of the fiscal deficit could ultimately hurt economic growth, Gupta said.
Government borrowing at high interest rates and its inability to slash subsidies and control rising expenditure were key factors contributing to the fiscal difficulties, economists said.
Fiscal consolidation, mainly that of states, was a daunting task and required changes in the constitution concerning fiscal relations between the federal and state governments.
A recent government report said India doled out subsidies worth more than 14 percent of GDP in 1994/95.
The report which urged reform of the subsidy system, said: "The macroeconomic costs of unjustified subsidies are mirrored in persistent large fiscal deficit and, consequently, higher interest rates."
The key to reducing subsidies was a phased increase in user charges, notably in prices for irrigation, power, transport, agriculture and industry.
"But removal of subsidies will be a political decision," Aashish Pitale, debt research manager at ICICI Securities and Finance Co, told Reuters.
The four left-wing parties in the coalition have been opposing the free market policies of the ruling United Front government.
"A slashing of subsidies will stoke inflation," said Gupta, adding this would affect the target of keeping inflation at 3.0-5.0 percent.
"It is a short-sighted view and absurd to think of inflation at 3.0-5.0 percent in the next three or four years," he said.

Economists said if the government made the rupee convertible on the capital account, there should be checks on flows of portfolio investment. Long term investors prefer the security of knowing that there is some control in place should there be any danger of a flight of capital.
"The countries which have attracted higher foreign direct investment are those which have controls on their capital account," Ghosh said.

India attracted foreign direct investment of $2.59 billion in 1996/97 against $1.93 billion in the previous year. Foreign institutional investment in 1996/97 stood at $2.39 billion compared with $2.04 billion in 1995/96.
